questions.prompt: What does owning a share of stock represent?
choices: A small piece of ownership in a company
A loan you made to a company
A guaranteed fixed payment every year
A membership fee to shop at a store
questions.explanation: A share makes you a part-owner, called a shareholder, of the company.

questions.prompt: People who own shares of a company are called shareholders.
questions.explanation: Owning shares gives you a slice of the company, which is exactly what a shareholder is.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: One unit of ownership in a company
A marketplace where shares are bought and sold
A share of profits paid to shareholders
questions.explanation: These four terms are the building blocks of how stock ownership works.

questions.prompt: Where are most public company stocks bought and sold?
choices: On stock exchanges like the NYSE or Nasdaq
At the company's front desk
Only inside local banks
Through the post office
questions.explanation: Exchanges like the NYSE and Nasdaq match up buyers and sellers of shares.

questions.prompt: Which of these can happen when you own shares of a company? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: You may receive dividends
You may get voting rights on some decisions
Your share value can rise or fall
The company guarantees you can never lose money
questions.explanation: Ownership can bring dividends, votes, and price changes, but never a guarantee against loss.

questions.prompt: A company splits its ownership into 1,000 shares and you own 50 of them. What percent of the company do you own?
questions.explanation: 50 out of 1,000 shares is 50 divided by 1,000, which equals 0.05, or 5%.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of buying your first stock in order.
items: Search for the company's ticker symbol
Place an order to buy shares
questions.explanation: You set up and fund an account, find the stock, then place your buy order.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a stock and a bond?
choices: A stock is ownership; a bond is a loan you make
A stock is a loan; a bond is ownership
They are two words for the exact same thing
Bonds can only be issued by tech companies
questions.explanation: Stocks make you an owner, while bonds make you a lender who gets paid back with interest.

questions.prompt: When you buy a government bond, you are lending money to the government.
questions.explanation: A bond is debt: the issuer borrows from you and pays you interest for the loan.

questions.prompt: Sort each feature under Stock or Bond.
items: Pays regular interest until it matures
May pay dividends and can grow a lot
Higher potential return with more ups and downs
questions.explanation: Stocks are equity with more growth and risk; bonds are debt with steadier, smaller returns.

questions.prompt: If a company goes bankrupt, who is generally paid first?
choices: Bondholders, because they are lenders
Shareholders, because they are owners
Whoever bought most recently
Nobody is ever paid anything
questions.explanation: Bondholders are creditors, so they line up ahead of shareholders when assets are paid out.

questions.prompt: Bonds usually offer higher potential returns and bigger price swings than stocks.
questions.explanation: It is the reverse: stocks usually have higher potential returns and more volatility than bonds.

questions.prompt: You buy a $1,000 bond that pays 4% interest per year. How many dollars of interest do you earn in one year?
questions.explanation: 4% of $1,000 is 0.04 times 1,000, which equals $40 of interest.

questions.prompt: Which are generally TRUE of bonds compared with stocks? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: They tend to be lower risk
They pay interest to the holder
They make you a part-owner of the company
They usually have smaller potential returns
questions.explanation: Bonds are lower-risk loans that pay interest with smaller returns, and they do not give ownership.

questions.prompt: What is the general relationship between risk and potential return?
choices: Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk
Higher returns always come with zero risk
Lower risk always means higher returns
Risk and return have nothing to do with each other
questions.explanation: To chase bigger gains you generally have to accept a bigger chance of loss. That is the risk-return tradeoff.

questions.prompt: Volatility describes how much an investment's price swings up and down.
questions.explanation: High volatility means bigger, faster price swings in both directions.

questions.prompt: Sort each asset into Lower risk or Higher risk.
questions.explanation: Insured cash and government bonds are steady, while individual stocks and crypto swing much more.

questions.prompt: Order these assets from LOWEST to HIGHEST typical risk.
questions.explanation: Cash is steadiest, then government bonds, then a broad stock fund, and a single stock is the riskiest.

questions.prompt: Which of these are ways to lower the risk in your investments? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Spread money across many different investments
Invest for a longer time horizon
Put all your money in one hot stock
Include some lower-risk assets like bonds
questions.explanation: Diversifying, staying invested longer, and mixing in steadier assets all cut risk; betting on one stock raises it.

questions.prompt: Why might a young investor accept more risk than someone about to retire?
choices: They have more time to recover from market drops
Young people never lose money
Risk disappears when you are young
Retirees automatically earn higher returns
questions.explanation: A longer time horizon gives markets more time to bounce back from downturns.

questions.prompt: An investment worth $200 grows to $230 in one year. What is the return, in percent?
questions.explanation: The $30 gain divided by the $200 you started with is 30 divided by 200, which equals 15%.

questions.prompt: What does diversification mean?
choices: Spreading your money across many different investments
Putting all your money in one stock
Only investing in a single industry
Keeping every dollar in cash
questions.explanation: Diversifying spreads risk so a single bad investment can't wipe you out.

questions.prompt: The saying 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' captures the idea of diversification.
questions.explanation: If you drop one basket you don't lose every egg, which is exactly what diversification protects against.

questions.prompt: How does an index fund make diversification easy?
choices: One purchase gives you tiny pieces of many companies at once
It guarantees you can never lose money
It only ever holds a single company
It removes the need for a brokerage account
questions.explanation: An index fund like an S&P 500 fund bundles hundreds of companies into one investment.

questions.prompt: Which of these portfolios are well diversified? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: A total-stock-market index fund
Shares of 500 companies across many industries
All your money in one airline stock
A mix of stocks and bonds from around the world
questions.explanation: Spreading across many companies, sectors, and asset types is diversified; one airline stock is not.

questions.prompt: Diversification can lower the risk of a single company doing badly, but it can't erase the risk of the whole market falling.
questions.explanation: Spreading out reduces company-specific risk, yet a market-wide drop still affects almost everything.

questions.prompt: An S&P 500 index fund holds roughly how many companies? Enter the number.
questions.explanation: The S&P 500 tracks about 500 of the largest U.S. companies inside a single fund.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A fund that holds all the companies in an index
An index of about 500 large U.S. companies
Putting most of your money in one place
questions.explanation: Diversification and index funds lower risk, while concentration raises it.

questions.prompt: What is a portfolio?
choices: The full collection of investments a person owns
A single stock
A type of bank loan
A government bond and nothing else
questions.explanation: Your portfolio is everything you hold together: stocks, bonds, funds, and cash.

questions.prompt: What does 'asset allocation' mean?
choices: How you divide your money among stocks, bonds, and cash
Choosing one single best stock
The fee a broker charges you
The tax you owe on your gains
questions.explanation: Asset allocation is the mix of asset types, and that mix shapes your risk and return.

questions.prompt: A common rule of thumb suggests putting about (110 minus your age)% in stocks. For a 20-year-old, what percent is that?
questions.explanation: 110 minus 20 equals 90, so the rule suggests roughly 90% in stocks for a 20-year-old.

questions.prompt: Younger investors are often encouraged to hold a larger share of stocks than people near retirement.
questions.explanation: With decades ahead, young investors can ride out market dips in exchange for higher long-run growth.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for building a beginner portfolio in order.
items: Set your goal and time horizon
Build an emergency fund of cash
Choose an asset allocation of stocks vs bonds
Buy diversified funds that match it
questions.explanation: Goal first, a safety cushion next, then pick a mix, invest in it, and check in yearly.

questions.prompt: What is 'rebalancing' a portfolio?
choices: Adjusting your holdings back to your target mix
Selling everything and starting over
Only ever buying and never selling
Moving your account to a new bank
questions.explanation: Over time winners grow and shift your mix, so rebalancing trims them back to your plan.

questions.prompt: Which factors should shape your asset allocation? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Your time horizon, meaning when you need the money
Your risk tolerance
Your goals
Your favorite color
questions.explanation: Time, comfort with risk, and goals drive your mix; your favorite color does not.

questions.prompt: A share of stock represents what?
choices: Part ownership of a company
A loan you made to a company
A guaranteed interest payment
A fee charged by your bank
questions.explanation: Stock is equity, which means it makes you a part-owner of the company.

questions.prompt: A bond is best described as what?
choices: A loan you make that pays you interest
A slice of company ownership
A savings account at a store
A share that always pays dividends
questions.explanation: A bond is debt: you lend money and earn interest until it is paid back.

questions.prompt: Stocks generally carry more risk and more growth potential than bonds.
questions.explanation: Equity swings more than bonds, but it can also grow more over the long run.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A share of profits paid to shareholders
How much a price swings up and down
How you split money among stocks, bonds, and cash
questions.explanation: These four terms are the core vocabulary of investing foundations.

questions.prompt: Sort each into Lower risk or Higher risk.
questions.explanation: Government bonds and insured cash are steady, while single stocks and crypto swing hard.

questions.prompt: You invest $500 and it grows to $575 in one year. What was your return, in percent?
questions.explanation: The $75 gain divided by the $500 you invested is 75 divided by 500, which equals 15%.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduce risk in a portfolio? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Diversifying across many investments
Adding some bonds to your mix
Putting everything in one stock
Investing for a longer time horizon
questions.explanation: Spreading out, adding steadier assets, and a longer horizon all cut risk; one stock raises it.

questions.prompt: Using the '110 minus age' rule, about what percent of a 30-year-old's portfolio would be in stocks?
questions.explanation: 110 minus 30 equals 80, so the rule suggests about 80% in stocks.

questions.prompt: Order these assets from LOWEST to HIGHEST typical risk.
questions.explanation: Cash is steadiest, bonds are next, a broad fund is higher, and a single stock is the riskiest.

questions.prompt: What does rebalancing a portfolio do?
choices: Returns your holdings to your target mix
Guarantees you a profit
Removes all risk from investing
Closes your investment account
questions.explanation: Rebalancing trims what has grown too big and tops up what has shrunk to keep your planned mix.
